\chapter{See You Again}
\label{ch:zh-zaijian}
\hlchaptermodality{6}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write \zh{再} and \zh{见}, say goodbye with \zh{再见}, read the word literally as \textquotedblleft{}see again\textquotedblright{} because its two pieces genuinely add up, and name which expressions I know are spoken differently from how they are written.}

The first exchange in the track that opens, turns and closes -- greeting, an answer either way, and a parting -- with every line built from characters the reader has written rather than a phrase memorised whole.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[zài]{\zh{再} — a bar, a frame, and a line that closes it}

\label{lesson:ZH-W06-zai}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{是}. Nine strokes, and the sun on top finished first.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\zh{再}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Six strokes.} Fewer than the last one, and the structure is easier to see: a horizontal bar across the top, a frame hanging underneath it, and a long horizontal closing the whole thing at the bottom.

1. the \textbf{top horizontal}, left to right 2. the \textbf{left side}, coming straight down 3. the \textbf{frame}: start again at the upper left, cross to the right, \textbf{turn down} the right side, and \textbf{hook left} at the base — all without lifting 4. the \textbf{central vertical}, down through the middle 5. the \textbf{inner horizontal}, left to right 6. the \textbf{long bottom horizontal}, left to right, wider than everything above it

Five pen lifts.

Stroke 3 is the one to watch. It is a \textbf{single stroke that changes direction twice} — across, down, then a hook to the left. You have met this before: the outer wall of a box is always one turning stroke, never two or three. Compare it with the frame you drew in \zh{日} and it is the same hand movement.

And the closing bar is last. \textbf{The box is not sealed until the end} — the same rule that made you draw the middle bar of \zh{日} before its bottom bar. Chinese stroke order keeps re-using a small set of habits, and this is one you now know well enough to expect.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{再} — bar, left side, then the turning frame in one movement
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{再} again, and count the lifts. There are five.
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{zài} — falling, from high to low
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which stroke of \zh{再} is drawn last? (\textbf{The long bottom bar}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jiàn]{\zh{见} — an eye on two legs}

\label{lesson:ZH-W06-jian}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{人}. Two strokes, left before right, a figure on two legs.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — the shape}
\begin{quote}
\zh{见}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Four strokes}, and after the last two characters that will feel like a rest.

It is built in two parts, top and bottom:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item on top, a \textbf{frame} — a narrow box, which the traditional reading takes to be an \textbf{eye}
  \item underneath, \textbf{two legs} — and they are the legs of \zh{人}, the walking figure you wrote first of all
\end{itemize}

The legs have changed a little in this position. The left one still falls away to the lower left exactly as it did. The right one no longer just presses down: it descends, \textbf{bends right along the base, and finishes with a hook upward}. That is what a leg does when it has to carry a frame above it.

The order:

1. the frame's \textbf{left side}, coming down 2. the frame's \textbf{top}, turning down the \textbf{right side} — one stroke, no lift 3. the \textbf{left leg}, falling to the lower left 4. the \textbf{right leg}: down, bend right, hook up — one stroke, no lift

Three pen lifts. Two of the four strokes turn, and neither of them is allowed to be broken into pieces.

\textbf{A frame over a person, and the word means \textquotedblleft{}to see.\textquotedblright{}} That is a memory hook, not a proof — but it is the kind of hook this book has been giving you in place of a shared ancestor with English, and this one is unusually easy to hold.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{人}, then \zh{见} — and find the legs in the second one
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{见}, stopping after stroke 2 to check the frame is closed on three sides
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{jiàn} — falling
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does the last stroke finish? (\textbf{With a hook, upward}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}; stroke order per the PRC standard \emph{Xiandai Hanyu Tongyongzi Bishun Guifan} (1997).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[zàijiàn]{\zh{再见} — the word that says what it means}

\label{lesson:ZH-C06-zaijian}



\begin{quote}
Write \zh{再}, then \zh{见}. Six strokes, then four.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\zh{再见}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\zh{再见}} \emph{zàijiàn} — \textbf{goodbye}. Two characters, one word, and you can already write both of them.

Now the meanings, which have been held back until you had the shapes:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\zh{再}} \emph{zài} means \textbf{again}
  \item \textbf{\zh{见}} \emph{jiàn} means \textbf{see}
\end{itemize}

So the word is \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}see again.\textquotedblright{}} That is not a hook, not a mnemonic, not a traditional gloss offered with a warning attached. It is what the two characters say, and it is what the word means.

Every earlier component in this book gave you a \emph{hook} — \zh{亻} at the left of \zh{你} because the word is about a person, \zh{女} beside \zh{子} in \zh{好} — honestly labelled as a memory aid rather than history. \textbf{\zh{再见} is different: the parts add up.} Chinese does this often. Start expecting it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{sounds}
Both syllables are \textbf{fourth tone}. Both fall.

Say it slowly: \emph{zài} falls, then \emph{jiàn} falls. Two separate drops, each starting high again. The common mistake is to run them into one long slide, which turns two syllables into a mumble. Reset your pitch upward between them. {[}REPEAT x2{]}

And nothing moves. Neither tone rule you have been taught applies to two fourth tones, so \textbf{\zh{再见} is said exactly as it is written.}
\end{sounds}

\begin{culture}
If you know any German: \emph{auf Wiedersehen} is \textquotedblleft{}on seeing again\textquotedblright{} — the same two pieces, in the same order.

That is a coincidence of thinking, not of ancestry; \textbf{Chinese and German share no common ancestor.} But parting by promising to meet again is an idea many languages reach for on their own, and that makes \zh{再见} far easier to hold than a shape memorised cold.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{zàijiàn} — two falls, resetting the pitch between them
  \item \emph{Read it:} \zh{再见} — give its literal reading before its translation
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Does either tone move in \zh{再见}? (\textbf{No — both fall, and nothing changes}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — a conversation that ends}

\label{lesson:ZH-C06-practice}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{zàijiàn}. Two falls, with the pitch reset between them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
Everything below is a character you have written yourself. Read it straight through:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{A:} \zh{你好}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{ní hǎo} — hello.
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{B:} \zh{你好}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{ní hǎo} — hello.
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{A:} \zh{是}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{shì} — is it?
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{B:} \zh{不是}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{bú shì} — no.
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{A:} \zh{再见}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{zàijiàn} — goodbye.
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\textbf{B:} \zh{再见}
\end{quote}

>

\begin{quote}
\emph{zàijiàn} — goodbye.
\end{quote}

That is a conversation with a beginning, a middle and an end. It is short, and it is real: two people meet, one asks something, the other declines it, and both leave properly. \textbf{Nothing in it is a phrase you memorised whole.} You built every line from characters and rules.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built — and what stays invisible}]
Read the exchange out loud once more, and count the places where your mouth does something the page does not record:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\zh{你好}} is written with two low dipping tones and spoken \emph{ní hǎo} — the first one rises.
  \item \textbf{\zh{不是}} is written with a falling \zh{不} and spoken \emph{bú shì} — the \zh{不} rises.
  \item \textbf{\zh{再见}} is written with two falls and spoken with two falls. Nothing moves.
\end{itemize}

Two out of three. That ratio is not a fluke, and it is the single most useful thing to know about reading Mandarin aloud: \textbf{the writing records the words, not the way the words meet each other.} From here on, whenever two pieces sit side by side, ask what happens between them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the whole exchange, both parts, without stopping
  \item \emph{Say it:} it again, taking B's side, and answer \zh{是} instead of \zh{不是}
  \item \emph{Write it:} \zh{再见} — six strokes, then four
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
In this exchange, how many of the three expressions are spoken exactly as written? (\textbf{One} — \zh{再见}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U4E00.pdf}{Unicode CJK Unified Ideographs chart}
\end{tcolorbox}
